shared_text:
The flight. A twin-engine airliner on an airline flight, departing at night. The report does not give the weather.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying for the take-off and the captain was the pilot monitoring.

What happened. The aircraft was cleared to line up and wait on the departure runway. The captain heard the tower tell another aircraft, landing on a different runway, to leave it by one taxiway and hold short of the departure runway on another. Shortly after the other aircraft read this back, the crew were cleared for take-off. The captain handed control to the first officer and, as the take-off roll began, kept watching the other aircraft, with a feeling that it was still moving too close to the hold-short line. It was in fact approaching the hold-short line for the departure runway. The two aircraft had similar-sounding callsigns. The tower controller urgently told the other aircraft to stop. The captain heard the instruction as "Stop!" addressed to their own aircraft. Recognising a possible conflict, the captain immediately took control and called "Reject". The speed was about 90 knots. The first officer took over as pilot monitoring, and the captain began to bring the aircraft to a stop.
safe_outcome: The captain brought the aircraft to a complete stop on the runway. The tower confirmed that the instruction to stop had been meant for the other aircraft. The crew taxied to the end of the runway and cleared it, completed the rejected take-off checklist and contacted maintenance, who confirmed there was no problem with the brake temperature system or the brake fuse plugs. After a short brake-cooling period the aircraft took off from another runway, and the rest of the flight was uneventful. The tower told the other aircraft to hold short of the departure runway, and an aircraft approaching to land on that runway went around. No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.
bad_outcome: The aircraft could not be stopped on the remaining runway. It left the end of the runway at about 30 knots and came to rest on the grass. The passengers were evacuated, and two received minor injuries during the evacuation. The aircraft was slightly damaged.
notes: Rule 3 removed: the controller's after-the-event remark that the similar callsigns "likely caused the miscommunication" (the similarity itself is kept as a fact) and the captain's "You told us to stop!" exchange. Rule 5 moved to the safe ending: the stop on the runway, the tower's clarification, taxiing clear, the QRH, the maintenance brake check and cooling, the later departure from another runway, ATC holding the other aircraft short, and the go-around of an aircraft approaching the departure runway (from narrative 2). Safe ending uses the D4 form because the report shows a traffic interaction. Judgement calls: (1) Narrative 2 is the account of the other (landing) aircraft's first officer, not this crew's. Its details (long float, incomplete readback, staying on the exit taxiway, handing over control) were left out of the shared text because this crew did not know them at the time; only the fact that the other aircraft was approaching the hold-short line was kept, which narrative 1 also confirms afterwards. (2) NASA's unstabilised-approach coding comes from narrative 2's long float; as instructed, the case is condensed as this crew's rejected take-off. (3) The weather is not in the report; "at night" is from the 0001-0600 local time block. (4) Bracket "end": an overrun after a rejection at about 90 knots is unlikely but possible in theory, the same point James made about pilot case 1.
